content: The larval stage of the parasite Taenia solium can form cysts in the central nervous system, leading to neurocysticercosis, which is the primary cause of acquired epilepsy in countries where the parasite is endemic. Endemic areas are defined as regions where the complete life cycle of T. solium is present or likely to occur. A meta-analysis published in 2010 estimated that neurocysticercosis lesions were detected via imaging in a median of 29% of patients presenting with epilepsy in endemic regions. The global burden of the disease was estimated to account for 8 million disability-adjusted life years (DALYs) in 2015. The impact of Taenia solium infections extends beyond health, encompassing significant economic costs for both humans and pigs (the intermediate host), as well as social costs, including discrimination and stigma faced by individuals with epilepsy. The parasite is most prevalent in impoverished and vulnerable communities where pigs roam freely, open defecation is practiced, basic sanitation is lacking, and health education is either absent or limited. The disease is predominantly found in Latin America, sub-Saharan Africa, and Asia. Several tools are available for controlling T. solium. Preventive chemotherapy (PC) targeting the adult tapeworm is one such tool. Other interventions include pig management, pig vaccination and treatment, improved sanitation and hygiene, and community education. These tools can be integrated under a One Health approach, which emphasizes collaboration across human, animal, and environmental health sectors to achieve more effective, efficient, and sustainable control of T. solium. The treatment of T. solium taeniasis using preventive chemotherapy is considered a core intervention for controlling the parasite, as it has an immediate effect in reducing the risk of neurocysticercosis transmission. However, prior to this guideline, no formal recommendations existed for the use of preventive chemotherapy for T. solium taeniasis. Program managers and stakeholders required updated, clear, and evidence-based guidance. This guideline was developed to provide such guidance. The recommendations are intended for a broad audience, including policymakers, technical advisors, and program staff involved in planning, implementing, monitoring, and evaluating preventive chemotherapy programs for T. solium control to improve public health. The objectives of the guideline are as follows: 1. To provide evidence-based recommendations on the appropriate choice of drug and dosage for preventive chemotherapy of T. solium in endemic areas. 2. To support the development of evidence-based national preventive chemotherapy strategies for T. solium by World Health Organization (WHO) Member States. 3. To promote a sustained and more efficient control of T. solium through the adoption of a One Health approach. The WHO guideline development process involves several steps, including planning, conducting a scoping and needs assessment, establishing internal and external guideline development groups, formulating key questions in the Population, Intervention, Comparison, Outcomes (PICO) format, commissioning systematic reviews, and formulating recommendations using the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation (GRADE) methodology.
